title: Papular urticaria & insect bites
summary: Recurrent itchy grouped papules from flea, mite or bed-bug hypersensitivity. Treat the source (pets, home, pest control) as well as the itch.

glance.think: Crops of very itchy firm papules in clusters or lines, often on a child’s legs or on exposed sleep sites — only one household member may react.
glance.engine: Immediate and delayed hypersensitivity to arthropod saliva; new bites can flare old lesions. Children usually desensitise over time.
glance.backbone: Eradicate the source (vet flea products + vacuum / professional bed-bug control) plus short topical steroid and antihistamine.
glance.never_miss: Anaphylaxis pathways for systemic allergy; fever after bites abroad; do not antibiotic-treat ordinary itchy redness lasting up to ~10 days.

what: Papular urticaria is a **chronic or recurrent eruption of intensely itchy grouped papules** (± vesicles). It is a hypersensitivity reaction to arthropod bites — most often **fleas**, mites, **bed bugs**, mosquitoes and gnats. Despite the name it is **not true urticaria** (lesions last days, not hours). It is commonest in children aged about 2–10.

list: Arthropod saliva triggers type I and type IV hypersensitivity. Bites are often unnoticed; reactions arrive hours to days later.
**Cat fleas** are the commonest fleas biting UK humans (even in dog-only homes). The home holds most of the eggs/larvae/pupae.
**Bed bugs** hide in mattress seams and feed at night; linked to travel and second-hand furniture.
Most children grow out of it as they desensitise.
Firm red itchy papules 3–10 mm, sometimes with a punctum, vesicle or blister; excoriation and later pigmentation are common.
Grouping in clusters or lines of three (“breakfast, lunch and dinner”).
Seasonal spring–autumn for fleas/outdoor insects; bed bugs all year.

head: Source
Clues
rows: Lower legs/ankles, waistband; pets; often only one person reacts; new house can awaken pupae
Face, neck, arms (exposed in bed); linear clusters; blood/faecal spots on sheets; travel

diagnosis: Clinical from morphology, grouping and history (pets, new house, travel, season). Find the source: flea-comb pets, inspect mattress seams. Investigations are rarely needed. Explain that only the sensitised person reacts.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Web spaces, wrists, genitals, burrows; whole household itchy
Wheals fade within 24 h; no crusted papules
Fever; crops at different stages including scalp
Conviction of infestation without confirming insects or lesions

list: **Fleas:** veterinary flea products for **all** pets; hot-wash bedding; vacuum thoroughly; household IGR spray for weeks.
**Bed bugs:** council pest control or BPCA/NPTA professional firm — home sprays rarely suffice.
Cool compresses, short nails, soap and water.
Non-sedating antihistamine by day; short sedating antihistamine at night if sleep is poor (check age licence).
Short mild-to-moderate **topical corticosteroid** on new itchy spots (potent short courses only on thick adult lesions).
Most bites do **not** need antibiotics — redness and itch can last ~10 days.
If spreading cellulitis/impetigo: flucloxacillin first-line (NICE NG182); Pharmacy First pathway for infected insect bites (England, age ≥1) within PGD rules.

red_flags: Systemically unwell, spreading cellulitis, immunocompromised with infection, bites in mouth/throat or around eyes.
Bites abroad with fever or persistent exotic lesion.
Atypical persistent eruption or suspected delusional infestation → GP/dermatology.
pearls: **The pet may look fine — the house is the reservoir.**
Antihistamines and steroids control symptoms; recurrences stop only when the source is gone.
Bed bug vs flea: sleep-exposed sites and linen spots vs ankles/pets.
Avoid long-term potent steroids and antibiotics without infection.
